A simple comic-strip storyboard (one box per broadcast) is a great way for them to plan the next one.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways Add sprites and backdrops from the libraries; each sprite has its own code. go to teleports; glide slides smoothly. broadcast + when I receive let sprites cue each other reliably. Plan the story out loud before coding it. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Built a project with multiple sprites and a backdrop Placed and moved sprites precisely with go to and glide Used broadcasts to make characters take turns reliably Coached a "story first, code second" project with your child 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save the story project and give it a good title Try the backdrop-change challenge, even with just one scene change Ask your child what kind of game they'd love to make — you'll need it next lesson Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage Our story got long and the scripts are hard to follow. Any tips? Name every broadcast clearly ( line 2 , scene: night ) and keep each sprite's scripts in a tidy column. Right-click the code area and choose Clean up Blocks to line everything up. Long stories are just many short cue-and-response pairs. Can we record our own voices for the characters? Yes! In a sprite's Sounds tab, hover over the Choose a Sound button and pick the microphone to record. Then use play sound until done in place of (or alongside) a say block. Kids love hearing their own voices come out of a character. My child wants to skip the planning and just start coding. Should I insist? Keep the plan tiny instead of skipping it — "Who's in it, where are they, and what's the first line?" takes one minute. Kids who start with no plan often get stuck on a blank screen; a one-minute plan gives them somewhere to go. 🔭 Looking Ahead In Lesson 3.2: A Simple Game with Variables & Score , you'll build the kind of project kids beg for — a real catch game. You'll meet the variable , the labeled box that remembers a score, and combine loops, if, sensing, and random numbers into something genuinely fun to play. Get ready to catch some falling apples. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You just directed a little animated film — cast, set, and cues. Coordinating several things at once is a real step up, and you did it. Every story your child makes from here builds on what you set up today. 🏠 Back to Course Home

label: Lesson 3.2
title: A Simple Game with Variables & Score

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: What's a variable?
sections.text: A variable is a labeled box that holds a value the computer can remember and change — like a score, a life count, or a player's name. The box has a name ("score") and a value (0, then 1, then 2…). Think of a whiteboard on the wall labeled "SCORE." You can read what's on it, erase it, and write a new number. That's a variable. Variables live in the orange Variables category. The three blocks you'll use constantly: set [score] to 0 — put a specific value in the box change [score] by 1 — add to what's already there [score] (the reporter) — read the current value

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Make a score variable
sections.text: Click the Variables category, then “Make a Variable.” Name it score , keep "For all sprites," and click OK. Figure 1: Making a variable. Name it clearly (like score ) and choose "For all sprites." Once created, a checkbox appears next to score in the palette — tick it and the score shows live on the stage. New blocks ( set , change , show/hide ) now use your variable.

sections.heading: 🗺️ The game plan
sections.text: Our game: apples fall from the top; move the cat with the mouse to catch them; each catch scores a point. Set the scene first: add an Apple sprite and keep the cat (or pick a "Bowl"). Optionally add a backdrop.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Code the apple
sections.text: Select the Apple sprite. It resets the score, then falls again and again from a random spot: when ⚑ clicked set score to 0 forever go to x: pick random -200 to 200 y: 170 repeat until touching Cat? change y by -8 if ⟨ y position ⟩ < -170 then go to x: pick random -200 to 200 y: 170 change score by 1 Read it as a story: start at the top at a random x, fall until caught (jump back to the top if it drops past the bottom), and when the cat catches it, add a point — then do it all again, forever. ⚠️ Why not "touching edge?" It's tempting to check touching edge? for "reached the bottom" — but the apple starts at y: 170 , where it's already touching the top edge. Scratch would send it back to the top every single frame and it would never fall. Checking y position < -170 means "near the bottom" and nothing else. (You'll use the same trick for falling stars in Module 4.) 💡 Where these came from pick random is a green Operators block. touching is a blue-green Sensing block; y position is at the bottom of Motion , and the < (less than) block is in Operators . repeat until and if are Control . You're combining four categories — real programming!

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Code the catcher
sections.text: Select the Cat . It simply follows the mouse left–right along the bottom: when ⚑ clicked forever go to x: mouse x y: -140 Press the green flag and move your mouse — the cat slides along the bottom, catching apples, and the score ticks up. You built a game! 🎉 ✅ Make it a real challenge Add a timer : make a time left variable, set it to 30, and in a loop change time left by -1 / wait 1 second until it hits 0, then broadcast game over and stop all . Now there's a reason to hurry. 🐛 Common problems & fixes Symptom Fix Score jumps up by lots at once The apple keeps touching the cat for several frames. After scoring, add go to the top immediately (as above) so it leaves the cat. Score never goes up Check the touching block names the right sprite, and the cat and apple actually overlap. Score doesn't reset Make sure set score to 0 runs on the green flag, before the forever loop. 🌱 Growth mindset: a harder project isn't a sign you've stopped improving If this lesson felt noticeably tougher than the last few, that's expected. You're juggling four block categories, a variable, and two sprites at once — the project got bigger, so it feels harder, even though your skills grew. Learning comes in steps and plateaus: stretches where nothing seems to click, then a sudden "oh!" when it all fits together. If the apple script still feels like a lot, rebuild it once from memory tomorrow; the second time is almost always easier. Tell your child the same thing when their big game idea feels overwhelming: "Big projects feel hard for everyone. Let's get one piece working, then the next."

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Design first, code second
sections.text: Games are where kids' ambitions outrun their skills — and where frustration lives. Head it off by designing on paper first . The one-page game design Goal: What are you trying to do? (Catch apples.) Controls: How do you play? (Move the mouse.) Scoring: How do you win/score? (+1 per catch.) Lose condition: Can you lose? (Timer runs out.) "Before we code, tell me your game like you're explaining it to a friend. How do you play? How do you win? Let's write those down — those are our to-do list." Explain variables with a real whiteboard Grab a sticky note labeled "SCORE: 0." Each time you pretend to catch something, cross it out and write the next number. Then say: "the change score by 1 block does exactly this." 👧 Ages 5–7 You build most of it; they choose the apple, the catcher, and press GO. The thrill is catching + watching the number grow. 🧒 Ages 8–11 They can build the catcher and add the score change. Great age to add the timer and a "game over" message. 🧑 Ages 12+ Push for levels, a high-score variable, or a "lives" system. Let them scope it — then help them cut it down to something finishable. ⚠️ The scope trap Kids dream up "an open-world game with 50 levels." Gently steer to one working mechanic first. "Let's make catching one apple perfect, then add more." A finished tiny game beats an abandoned huge one — for their motivation and yours.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: What is a variable? Question 2: To add one point to the score, you use… Question 3: Where should "set score to 0" go?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down Grab the same notebook or notes app you've been using. A few honest lines now will make the next lesson easier — and give you a record of how far you've come. Key concepts: Describe a variable using your own everyday comparison (a whiteboard? a scoreboard? a jar of marbles?). What's the difference between set and change ? What clicked: Was it the score ticking up for the first time? Seeing pick random send the apple somewhere new each drop? Questions & confusion: Does the repeat until loop inside the forever make sense yet? Write down which part of the apple script you'd want to re-read. Ideas to try: One rule you'd add: a timer, lives, faster apples as the score rises, or a "bad" object to avoid. Progress & feelings: This was the biggest build so far. How did it feel to juggle it all? How did your child react when the game actually worked? 💡 Teach It tip: Tape your child's one-page game design (goal, controls, scoring, lose condition) into their notebook, and have them check off each part as it starts working. It turns a big project into a visible to-do list — and a record of how much they finished.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways A variable is a named box that stores a changeable value like a score. set puts a value in; change adds to it; tick the checkbox to show it on stage. A game combines loops, if, sensing, operators, and variables together. Design on paper first, build one working mechanic, then grow it. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Created your first variable and used it to keep score Combined loops, if, sensing, operators, and variables into a working game Showed a live score on the stage Coached a "design first, code second" game project 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save the catch game — you'll use it to practice debugging next lesson Try adding the 30-second timer challenge Let your child play-test it and suggest one improvement Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage What's the difference between "For all sprites" and "For this sprite only"? "For all sprites" makes one shared score every sprite can read and change — perfect for a score or timer. "For this sprite only" gives that sprite its own private copy. When in doubt, pick "For all sprites"; that's what almost every beginner game needs. My child wants more apples falling at once. Do we copy the apple sprite? Duplicating the sprite (right-click → duplicate ) works, but every copy has its own code to keep in sync. Scratch has a much neater tool for this called clones — one sprite that makes many copies of itself — and it gets a full lesson in Module 4. The game is fun but my child already wants lives, levels, and a boss. How do I handle that? Write every idea on a "someday" list so nothing is lost, then pick just one to add next. Finishing small upgrades one at a time keeps the game working and the motivation high. Several of those ideas — lives, a game-over screen, and a reset — are part of the capstone game in Module 4. 🔭 Looking Ahead Every project hits bugs, and the best coders are the best fixers . In Lesson 3.3: Debugging & Remixing you'll learn a calm, kid-friendly method for tracking down problems, plus how to learn from others with See Inside and remixing. Hang on to this apple game, too: in Module 4 you'll grow the same idea into Star Catcher , with clones, lives, and a proper game-over screen. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You built a real, playable game with a scoreboard — something plenty of adults assume they could never do. If it stretched you, good: that stretch is exactly where the learning happens. Rest, play your game, and come back ready. 🏠 Back to Course Home

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The debugging mindset
sections.text: Professional programmers spend more time fixing than writing. "Bug" is just the word for "not doing what I expected yet." The single most valuable thing you can model for your child is calm curiosity in the face of a bug. The computer isn't wrong and it isn't being mean. It's doing exactly what the blocks say. Debugging is the detective game of finding the gap between what you said and what you meant. ✅ Reframe the language Swap "It's broken / I failed" for "Interesting — let's find out why." Bugs become puzzles instead of defeats. This one habit protects a child's confidence for years. 🌱 Growth mindset: every bug is feedback, not a verdict A bug is the computer giving you precise, honest feedback: "here is exactly what your blocks told me to do." It isn't a judgment about whether you're a "computer person." Each one you track down teaches you something you'll never have to learn again — which is why experienced coders are mostly people who have made a lot of mistakes and paid attention to them. Let your child hear you say, "Ooh, a bug — what is it telling us?" When grown-ups treat mistakes as clues instead of failures, kids learn it's safe to try hard things.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The 4-step method
sections.text: When something's wrong, resist random flailing. Walk this loop instead: The golden rule is step 3: change only one thing at a time , then test. Change five things and you'll never know which one mattered. 🔍 Scratch's built-in debugging helpers Click a block or stack to run just that piece and watch what it does. Tick a variable's checkbox to watch its value change live on the stage. Add a temporary "say" block to print a value: say (score) tells you what the computer "thinks." Slow it down with wait blocks so you can see each step.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The usual suspects
sections.text: 90% of Scratch bugs are one of these. Keep this table handy: Symptom Usual cause Fix Nothing happens Code is on the wrong sprite Select the right sprite in the sprite list Runs once, never reacts again An if with no loop around it Wrap the check in a forever loop Blocks after a loop never run Trapped below a forever Move them inside, or use repeat until Sprite zooms off / upside-down Position not reset / rotation style Add go to x/y at start; set rotation to left-right Score jumps by many at once Condition stays true for many frames Move the sprite away, or add a short wait after scoring Two sprites out of sync Relying on wait timing Coordinate with broadcast / when I receive

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: See Inside & remixing
sections.text: One of Scratch's superpowers: you can look at the code of almost any shared project . On a project's page, click “See Inside” to open its full code and explore how it was made — a bottomless, free learning resource. Figure 1: A shared project page. See Inside (top-right) reveals the code; the icons show loves, favorites, remixes, and views. Remixing means making your own copy of someone's project to change and build on. Click See Inside , then Remix (when signed in), and it becomes yours to modify. Scratch is built around this — it's encouraged, not frowned upon. ✅ Remixing done right Change something meaningful and make it your own. Scratch auto-credits the original — leave that intact. Thank the original creator in your notes. ⚠️ Talk with your child about Remixing to learn , not to claim someone's work as fully theirs. It's normal (and great) to learn by studying others' code. Reading other people's code is how every programmer improves. "See Inside" turns the whole Scratch community into your child's textbook.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Coaching through frustration
sections.text: A bug plus a tired kid equals tears. Your calm is the most important debugging tool in the room. The "rubber duck" trick Have your child explain their code out loud, block by block, to you (or a stuffed animal). Astonishingly often, they find the bug themselves mid-sentence — just from saying it aloud. "Walk me through it like I know nothing. What should this block do? …and what did it actually do?" Ask, don't fix "What did you expect to happen?" "What happened instead ?" "Which block do you think is responsible?" "What's one thing we could change to test that?" Know when to take a break If frustration boils over, stop. "Let's let our brains rest — coders do this all the time." Walking away and coming back fresh is a real, professional debugging strategy, not giving up. 👧 Ages 5–7 Keep bugs tiny and fixes fast. Celebrate the fix dramatically: "You SQUASHED the bug!" 🐞 🧒 Ages 8–11 Teach the 4-step method explicitly. Let them lead; you ask the questions. Introduce "See Inside" on a project they love. 🧑 Ages 12+ Encourage remixing an ambitious project to learn a new technique, then bringing that idea back to their own work. ⚠️ The biggest parent mistake Grabbing the mouse and fixing it yourself. It ends the frustration and the learning. Sit on your hands; ask one more question. The pride of their fix is the whole point.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: The golden rule of debugging is… Question 2: What does "See Inside" do on a shared project? Question 3: Your child is melting down over a stubborn bug. Best move?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down Grab the same notebook or notes app you've been using. A few honest lines now will make the next lesson easier — and give you a record of how far you've come. Key concepts: Write the 4-step method (Watch → Predict → Change one thing → Test) from memory. Why does changing only one thing matter so much? What clicked: Which "usual suspect" have you already run into in your own projects? Did the table explain a bug you'd fixed by luck? Questions & confusion: Anything unclear about remixing etiquette, or how See Inside and Remix differ? Ideas to try: Find one shared project your child loves, click See Inside , and note one technique you'd like to borrow. Progress & feelings: How do you react when code breaks — and has that changed since Module 1? How did your child handle their last bug? 💡 Teach It tip: Start a "Bug Hall of Fame" page in your child's notebook: for each bug, write what it did, what caused it, and how they squashed it. Kids love watching the list grow — and it quietly teaches that bugs are trophies, not failures.

sections.heading: Summary & Module 3 Complete 🎉
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways Bugs are normal. Model calm curiosity, not frustration. Debug with a loop: Watch → Predict → Change one thing → Test . Most bugs are a handful of usual suspects — keep the table handy. See Inside and remixing turn the whole community into a learning resource. 🏆 Module 3 done! You've built a story and a game, and you can fix things when they wobble. That's a genuinely capable coding buddy. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Learned a calm, repeatable 4-step debugging method Can spot the most common Scratch bugs and fix them Used See Inside to learn from the Scratch community Finished Module 3: a story, a game, and the skills to fix them 📋 Before the Next Lesson Deliberately break your catch game (move one block) and let your child debug it Explore one shared project with See Inside together Save your apple game — its ideas return in the Module 4 capstone Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage My child gets upset and says "I'm bad at this" when a bug appears. What do I say? Separate the bug from the person: "The code has a bug; you're a coder who's finding it." Point to bugs they've already fixed — a Bug Hall of Fame helps here. And if emotions are high, take a short break; that's a real debugging strategy, not quitting. Is remixing the same as copying? I don't want to teach my child to cheat. Remixing is openly encouraged on Scratch: everything shared there is under a license that allows it, and Scratch automatically credits the original creator. The line to teach is honesty — change something meaningful, keep the credit, and don't pretend the whole thing is yours. I can't find the bug even after trying the 4 steps. Now what? Shrink the problem. Pull blocks off the script until the smallest piece that still misbehaves is left, or click individual blocks to run them one at a time. Explaining it aloud to a "rubber duck" works for adults too. And sometimes the best move is simply to come back tomorrow with fresh eyes. 🔭 Looking Ahead Module 4: Leveling Up — Bigger Projects begins with Lesson 4.1: Clones — One Sprite, Many Copies , the neat way to make lots of falling objects without duplicating sprites. Then you'll learn to make your own custom blocks with My Blocks , and bring it all together in a capstone you plan and build as a team: Star Catcher , a complete game with falling stars, a score, lives, and a game-over screen. Your new debugging skills will get plenty of use. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You now know how to build things and how to fix them when they go wrong — that second skill is the one that makes a real coder. Three modules down. Take a moment to notice how much of this would have looked like gibberish when you started. 🏠 Back to Course Home

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why one sprite isn't enough
sections.text: In the apple game from Lesson 3.2, one apple fell at a time. What if you wanted twenty ? You could duplicate the sprite twenty times — until you decide the apples should fall faster and have to edit all twenty. Clones fix this. A clone is a copy of a sprite that Scratch makes while the program is running . You write the code once; the sprite makes as many copies as it needs, then throws them away. Think of a rubber stamp . The stamp stays in your hand; each press leaves a print . Change the stamp, and every print after that changes too. In Scratch, the original sprite is the stamp, and clones are the prints.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The three clone blocks
sections.text: All three live at the very bottom of the orange Control category, below the loops and if blocks. Figure 1: “when I start as a clone” peeks in at the bottom of Control; the other two clone blocks sit just below. Block What it does Stamp analogy create clone of [myself] Makes a new copy of the sprite right now Press the stamp down when I start as a clone A hat block that runs only on each new clone — never the original What each print does after it lands delete this clone Removes the clone that runs it Wipe the print away The original (the stamp) when ⚑ clicked hide forever create clone of myself wait 1 seconds Each clone (the prints) when I start as a clone show say I'm a copy! for 2 seconds delete this clone This two-script shape is the pattern for almost every clone project. Don't skip the wait — without it, the loop stamps clones as fast as the computer can go. The stamping loop runs forever; the clone steps happen once for every clone, all at the same time.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: How clones behave
sections.text: Four rules explain almost every clone surprise: A clone is born as an exact copy of the original — same spot, direction, costume, size, and effects. It even copies being hidden . So move the original before stamping, and start the clone script with show . Each clone runs its own copy of the clone script , side by side, each minding its own business. "when 🟩 clicked" runs only on the original. Clones are made after the flag is clicked, so they miss it. (Hats like when I receive and when this sprite clicked run on the original and every clone.) Always clean up. Scratch allows about 300 clones at once; after that, create clone quietly does nothing. Off-screen clones still count, so every clone needs a way to reach delete this clone . The red stop sign clears them all.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Build falling stars
sections.text: Let's put the pattern to work: a new star every second, appearing at a random spot along the top and drifting down. 💡 Before you start Start a new project. Hover over the cat face button in the bottom-right corner, click Choose a Sprite , and pick Star . A dark backdrop such as Stars or Night City makes the stars pop. Program the stamp (the original) With the Star selected, build this. The original hides, then forever jumps to a random spot along the top, stamps a clone, and waits. when ⚑ clicked hide forever go to x: pick random -220 to 220 y: 180 create clone of myself wait 1 seconds Click the green flag. Nothing visible happens — and that's correct! The clones exist, but they're hidden, like prints in invisible ink. Program the prints (each clone) In the same Star sprite, start a second script. Each clone shows itself, falls to near the bottom, then deletes itself. when I start as a clone show repeat until ⟨ y position ⟩ < -170 change y by -5 delete this clone The less-than block is in green Operators ; drop the blue y position reporter (bottom of Motion ) into its left slot and type -170. Run it Click the green flag. Stars keep appearing and falling, many at once. Press stop and they all vanish. 🤔 Why not "until touching edge"? Each star is born touching the top edge, so it would delete itself instantly. Checking y position means "stop near the bottom." ✅ Hold on to this project! Save it. These falling stars are the heart of Star Catcher , the game you'll build in Lesson 4.3: a bowl slides along the bottom, each clone checks "am I touching the bowl?" to score, and stars that reach the bottom cost a life.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Make it yours
sections.text: Every clone runs its own script, so each one can be different: 🎨 Easy Change wait 1 to wait 0.3 — a meteor shower! Add turn ↻ 5 degrees inside the repeat so the stars spin as they fall. 🔥 A bit more Random sizes and colors: add the two Looks blocks below, before show . when I start as a clone set size to pick random 30 to 100 % change color effect by pick random 0 to 200 show repeat until ⟨ y position ⟩ < -170 change y by -5 delete this clone 💡 Challenge: let it snow Paint a small white circle, make its clones fall slowly, and add change x by (pick random -2 to 2) inside the loop so each flake drifts. Same pattern, new look — proof you've learned the idea .

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix Nothing appears at all Clones copy the hidden original, and the clone script never says show Put show right under when I start as a clone Stars pile up in one spot, or a huge clump appears The original never moves before stamping, or the loop has no wait Add go to x: (pick random) y: 180 before create clone , and a wait after it Game slows down, then new stars stop appearing Clones are never deleted and hit the 300 limit End every clone with delete this clone The original falls too The falling code is under when 🟩 clicked Move it under when I start as a clone When clones misbehave, ask first: "Is this code running on the stamp, on the prints, or on both?" 🌱 Growth mindset: confusion is the feeling of your brain stretching Clones are the first idea here where lots happens at once, so a crowded, fuzzy feeling is normal — it's what learning something genuinely new feels like. Adults often hide that feeling from kids. Try the opposite: "This part is tricky for me. Let's slow down and figure out which stars are doing what." Your child learns that "tricky" means "work through it," not "I'm bad at this."

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Stamps and prints
sections.text: Clones are abstract. Make them physical first. Start with a real stamp A rubber stamp or a cookie cutter and play-dough works. Make a few prints, then ask: "Where's the stamp now? In my hand, not on the paper. In Scratch, the original star hides like the stamp, and the falling stars are prints. What should each print do after it lands?" Let them discover the "invisible ink" bug When the stamp script shows nothing, resist fixing it. Ask: "We hid the stamp. The prints are copies of the stamp… so what do the prints look like right now?" 👧 Ages 5–7 Copies popping into existence feels like magic — that's enough. You build the scripts; they pick the sprite, the backdrop, and the falling speed. 🧒 Ages 8–11 They build both scripts with you nearby. The random size and color challenge shows that each clone runs its own copy of the code. 🧑 Ages 12+ Challenge them to spawn enemies that enter from the right and chase the player. Ask them to explain why their clones get deleted. ⚠️ Common kid bug Kids often put create clone of myself inside the clone's own script, so every clone makes another and the screen floods. Ask: "Who should do the stamping — the stamp or the prints?"

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: The original star is hidden. You make clones, but none appear on the stage. Why? Question 2: Which script runs only on the new clones, never on the original? Question 3: Your falling-stars game gets slower and slower, and then new stars stop appearing. The most likely cause?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down Clones are a big step up. Writing it down now will make Lesson 4.3 much easier. Key concepts: In your own words, how is a clone different from the original? What does each clone block do? What clicked: The stamp idea? The first falling star? Realizing why the clones were invisible? Questions & confusion: Which rule still feels slippery — what clones copy, which hats run where, or why deleting matters? Ideas to try: What else comes in crowds — fish, balloons, falling pizza? Sketch the stamp and the prints. Progress & feelings: How did managing many things at once feel? How did your child react when the sky filled with stars? 💡 Teach It tip: Have your child draw a big stamp with arrows to lots of little stars, labeled "original" and "clones," then explain the picture back to you.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways A clone is a copy of a sprite made while the program runs — the original is the stamp, clones are the prints. The pattern: the hidden original stamps clones in a forever loop with a wait ; each clone uses when I start as a clone to show , do its job, and delete this clone . Clones copy the original's position, look, and visibility; "when 🟩 clicked" runs only on the original. Scratch allows about 300 clones, so always delete the ones you're done with. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Used all three clone blocks in a real project Built a shower of falling stars from one sprite Learned the rules behind most clone bugs 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save your falling-stars project for Lesson 4.3 Try one "make it yours" change with your child Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage Is my child too young for clones? Not for enjoying them — young kids love watching copies appear while you build. The deeper rules usually land around age 8 or 9. Can each clone have its own speed or number? Yes. A variable created as "For this sprite only" gives every clone its own private copy. It's a great next step for older kids once variables feel comfortable. Should we just duplicate sprites instead? It seems simpler. For a few characters that behave differently, duplicating is fine. If you catch yourself making Star4 and Star5, it's time for clones. 🔭 Looking Ahead In Lesson 4.2: My Blocks — Make Your Own Blocks , you'll bundle a stack of blocks into one custom block with a name you choose, like jump or reset game . Then, in Lesson 4.3, your falling stars and custom blocks come together in Star Catcher . 💛 Encouragement for the Journey A few weeks ago you'd never snapped two blocks together. Today you told a computer to create, move, and clean up dozens of objects on its own. That's real programming. 🏠 Back to Course Home

label: Lesson 4.2
title: My Blocks — Make Your Own Blocks

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Why make your own blocks?
sections.text: As projects grow, the same few blocks keep showing up: a jump here, the same jump there, another copy for when the cat touches something. Long, repetitive scripts are hard to read, and changing the jump means hunting down every copy. Think of a recipe card that says "Make pancakes." Those two words stand for a whole list of steps: crack the eggs, whisk, pour, flip. Once the card is written, you just say "make pancakes." A custom block works the same way. You write the steps once , give them a name, and from then on one block stands for all of them. Programmers call a named chunk of code a function . Your child doesn't need the word, but you're doing exactly what professional coders do every day. Three scripts say "jump," but the jumping steps live in one place. Change them there, and every jump changes.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The Make a Block dialog
sections.text: Click the pink My Blocks circle at the bottom of the block categories, then the Make a Block button. A dialog opens with a pink block that says block name . Name your block Type a short action word that says what it does , like jump . Add an input (optional) Add an input (number or text) puts a slot in your block so you can hand it a value each time, like how many times to dance. You name the slot, for example times . (The boolean input is for yes/no values; skip it for now.) Add a label (optional) Add a label adds plain words between inputs so the block reads like a sentence, for example dance (times) times . Decide on "Run without screen refresh" Normally Scratch redraws the stage each time through a loop, so you watch things move. Tick this box and the whole block runs in one go, showing only the end result. Handy for setup, but animations happen instantly (you never see the jump!). Leave it unticked . Click OK . Two things appear: your new block in the My Blocks palette, and a pink define hat block in the code area.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The define block
sections.text: The define block is your recipe card: whatever you snap underneath it is what your new block does. On its own it never runs; it waits until another script uses the block. 📝 The recipe (define) define jump The steps go under here. 🗣️ Using it (the call) when ⚑ clicked jump Drag it from My Blocks like any other block. Using the block is called calling it: the green flag script calls jump, Scratch runs the define script's steps, then comes back and carries on.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Mini-project 1 — a jump block
sections.text: Start a new project with the cat. Make a block named jump (no inputs, screen refresh unticked) and build this under the define hat: define jump repeat 10 change y by 10 repeat 10 change y by -10 Up ten little steps, down ten little steps. Now give the player a way to use it: when space key pressed jump Press space and the cat hops. Now add a when this sprite clicked → jump script too: two ways to jump, one set of steps. Want a higher jump? Change the define script once, and both scripts get it.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Mini-project 2 — add an input
sections.text: An input lets one block do slightly different things. Click Make a Block , type dance , click Add an input (number or text) and name it times , then Add a label and type times . Click OK. The new define block contains a round pink times oval: the input's value. Drag it out of the define block (you get a copy) into the repeat slot: define dance times times repeat times turn ↻ 15 degrees wait 0.2 seconds turn ↺ 15 degrees wait 0.2 seconds Your palette block now has a white slot for any number: when ⚑ clicked dance 3 times say Ta-da! for 1 seconds dance 6 times On the recipe card, the input is "how many pancakes?" Same steps, different number. 💡 Challenge: make jump (height) Right-click the define block → Edit and add a number input called height . Use the Operators block (height / 10) as the "change y by" amount going up, and (0 − (height / 10)) going down. Now jump (50) is a hop and jump (150) a leap.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: A reset game block
sections.text: Some of the most useful blocks simply tidy up. Every game puts things back to the start when the green flag is pressed, and that setup list gets long. Wrap it in a block called reset game : define reset game set score to 0 set lives to 3 go to x: 0 y: -150 show when ⚑ clicked reset game (Make the score and lives variables first, as in Lesson 3.2.) Now the green flag script reads like plain English. ⭐ You'll use this in the capstone In Lessons 4.3–4.4 , starting with Capstone Part 1 — Plan It & Build the Core , you and your child build Star Catcher : a bowl catching falling star clones from Lesson 4.1. The bowl's reset game block is exactly this one. 💡 My Blocks belong to one sprite A custom block only appears in the palette of the sprite you made it in. To reuse it, drag the define script onto the other sprite's picture in the sprite list; it copies over.

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix Using the block does nothing The steps are sitting loose, not attached to the define hat Drag them until they snap under the define hat The input is always blank or 0 The oval came from somewhere else, or was never placed Drag the input oval out of the define block itself into the slot My block isn't in the palette A different sprite is selected Select the sprite you made it in, or drag the define script onto the other sprite The jump or dance happens instantly "Run without screen refresh" is ticked Right-click the define block → Edit → untick it 🌱 Growth mindset: going back isn't going backward Cleaning up code that already works can feel like admitting the first version was "wrong." It isn't. Programmers call it refactoring and do it constantly, because every project teaches a better way. When your child spots a repeated chunk in an old game, say: "Look how much you've grown — you can see things now you couldn't last month." Then say the same about your own projects.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: New words for the computer
sections.text: For kids, the big idea isn't "functions." It's that they invent new words and the computer learns them. Start with a game of "new word" Before touching the computer, play it out loud: "I'm going to teach you a new word: zoomba . Zoomba means clap twice and spin around. Ready? Zoomba! …Now let's teach the computer a new word." Let them find the repeats When the same blocks appear twice, don't point it out. Ask: "I see those same blocks twice. What would you call what they do? What if that were one block with that name?" The name is theirs ("boing" is perfect; silly names stick), and so is the number: let them try dance 1, dance 20, dance 100. 👧 Ages 5–7 "Teaching the computer a new word." Build the define script together; they pick the name and use the block. Skip inputs. 🧒 Ages 8–11 They can build jump and dance alone. Introduce inputs with dance (times), then challenge them to invent a block like sneeze or celebrate . 🧑 Ages 12+ Have them refactor their Lesson 3.2 game, replacing setup and repeated chunks with named blocks, then explain why it's easier to change. ⚠️ Common kid bug They type "times" into a slot instead of dragging the oval out, so Scratch sees the word , not the number. Point at the pink oval: "The value lives in here — drag it out."

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: Where do you put the steps that your new block should do? Question 2: Your jump block works, but the cat seems to teleport instead of hopping. What's the likely cause? Question 3: You made a reset game block on the Bowl sprite, but it's missing when you click the Star sprite. Why?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down A notebook or notes app works. Writing things down helps them stick, and lets you look back and see how far you've come. Key concepts: In your own words, what's the difference between the define block and using it? What does an input add? What clicked: The recipe card, two scripts sharing one jump, or dance 3 becoming dance 6? Questions & confusion: Is dragging the input oval still fuzzy? Screen refresh? Note exactly where you got stuck. Ideas to try: Name one block you wish Scratch had. Could you build it now? Progress & feelings: How does it feel to make blocks instead of just using them? What did your child name their first one? 💡 Teach It tip: Have your child start a "dictionary" page: each block they invent, with its name and a drawing of what it does.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways A custom block (a function ) names a chunk of code so you write it once . Make a Block sets the name, inputs, and labels; leave Run without screen refresh unticked. Steps go under the define hat; drag the input oval out of it to use its value. My Blocks belong to one sprite; drag the define script to share it. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Made your first custom block and used it from two scripts Built a block with an input that changes its behavior Wrote a reset game block ready for the capstone 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save your project with the reset game block Keep your falling-star clones project from Lesson 4.1 handy Ask your child for one idea to add to a catching game ❓ Common Questions at This Stage Is this too advanced for my 6-year-old? Not the idea: young kids get "teaching the computer a new word" right away. Skip inputs, build the define script together, and let them enjoy using the block they named. When should we make a custom block instead of just copying blocks? If you've copied the same group of blocks twice, or a script no longer fits on screen, give that chunk a name. There's no penalty for doing it later. I renamed my block and now things look different. Did I break something? Probably not. When you edit a block, Scratch updates every place it's used automatically, which copied blocks can't do. 🔭 Looking Ahead Next is the big one: the two-part capstone (Lessons 4.3–4.4), starting with Lesson 4.3: Capstone Part 1 — Plan It & Build the Core . You'll combine arrow-key controls, falling star clones, score and lives, and your reset game block into Star Catcher , planning it on paper with your child first. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You're no longer just using Scratch's tools — you're making your own. That's a real shift, and your child gets to watch you make it.

label: Lesson 4.3
title: Capstone Part 1 — Plan It & Build the Core

sections.heading: 🎬 What we're building
sections.text: In Star Catcher , stars fall from random spots at the top of the screen and you slide a bowl with the arrow keys to catch them. Each catch adds to your score ; each miss costs one of three lives ; at zero lives, GAME OVER . It uses nearly everything you've learned: Game piece Idea it uses Where you learned it Bowl moves with arrow keys forever + if + key pressed Lesson 2.3 Score and lives Variables Lesson 3.2 Lots of falling stars Clones Lesson 4.1 One block that resets the game My Blocks Lesson 4.2 Game Over appears Broadcasts Lesson 3.1 That's a lot for one sitting, so it's split on purpose. Today: plan it and build a playable game with a score. Part 2: lives, Game Over, and a launch.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Plan before you code
sections.text: The most important skill today isn't a block; it's planning . Games started by dragging blocks tend to grow too big to finish. Five minutes on paper prevents that: Brainstorm. Lots of ideas, no judging. Silly is welcome ("a taco that dodges forks!"). Pick ONE small idea with one main action: catch, dodge, jump, or chase. Other ideas go on a "someday list." Sketch it on paper. Where does the player start? What moves? How do you score, and how do you lose? List the pieces as a checklist. Every sprite, variable, and rule becomes a line to tick off. Build the smallest playable version first, then add one thing at a time. That last step is a loop game studios use too: Test after every addition, and any bug came from the one thing you just added. 🌱 Growth mindset: small is how big things start Shrinking a grand idea into "a bowl catches stars" can feel like a letdown. It isn't. Every big game started as a tiny, plain version that barely worked. Say it out loud when you trim the plan: "We're not throwing this idea away. We're building the part we can finish first." Your child learns that a finished small thing beats an unfinished giant one, and learns it by watching you.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: The game design card
sections.text: Copy this card onto paper and fill it in together. Our Star Catcher answers are on the right. 🃏 Game Design Card Question Our answer (Star Catcher) Game name Star Catcher Who is the player? A bowl at the bottom of the screen Controls: how do you move? Left and right arrow keys What else moves? Stars fall from random spots at the top How do you score? Catch a star: +1 point and a "pop" sound How do you lose? A star hits the ground: lose 1 of 3 lives What happens at the end? GAME OVER appears and the game stops Smallest playable version Bowl moves + stars fall + catching adds score Someday list (later ideas) Faster stars, rocks to dodge, high score, levels ✏️ Sketch box: leave space to draw the stage: bowl at the bottom, stars at the top, arrows for movement. Then write the checklist of pieces : Bowl sprite, Star sprite, Game Over sprite, score , lives , a reset game block, and a game over broadcast. Seven ticks. Today covers all but the two Game Over pieces. The someday list becomes Part 2's bonus menu.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Build the core game
sections.text: Press the green flag after every step. Times are for a parent alone; with a child driving, expect about double, and that's fine. These seven steps build the smallest playable version . Set the stage (about 4 min) Start a new project and delete the cat (right-click → delete ). Use Choose a Sprite to add a Bowl and a Star , and pick a night-sky backdrop such as "Stars." Make the variables (about 3 min) In Variables , click Make a Variable , name it score , and choose For all sprites . Repeat for lives (it gets used in Part 2). Leave both ticked so they show on the stage. Build the reset game block on the Bowl (about 6 min) Select the Bowl . In My Blocks , click Make a Block , type reset game , and click OK. A pink define hat appears. Snap these under it: define reset game set score to 0 set lives to 3 go to x: 0 y: -150 show It's the same block from Lesson 4.2. Make the Bowl move (about 6 min) Still on the Bowl, call reset game once, then check the arrow keys forever: when ⚑ clicked reset game forever if key right arrow pressed? then change x by 10 if key left arrow pressed? then change x by -10 Click the green flag, then the stage, and tap the arrows. The bowl slides; score and lives show 0 and 3. Turn the Star into a star factory (about 5 min) Select the Star . The original never falls; it hides and makes clones, like a factory behind the curtain: when ⚑ clicked hide wait 1 seconds forever create clone of myself wait pick random 0.5 to 1.5 seconds The first wait lets the player get ready; the random wait keeps the rhythm unpredictable. Make each clone fall (about 6 min) Add a second Star script. Each new clone jumps to a random spot along the top, appears, and falls: when I start as a clone go to x: pick random -220 to 220 y: 170 show forever change y by -5 Stars rain down! They pile up at the bottom for now; Part 2 turns misses into lost lives. Catch the stars (about 5 min) Inside the clone's forever loop, under change y by -5 , add a catching check. First add Pop (or any sound) in the Star's Sounds tab. when I start as a clone go to x: pick random -220 to 220 y: 170 show forever change y by -5 if touching Bowl? then change score by 1 hide play sound Pop until done delete this clone Why not just start sound ? Deleting a clone silences its sound, cutting off the pop. Hiding makes the star vanish instantly; until done lets the pop finish before the clone goes. ✅ Checkpoint: it's a real game! Play it. Stars fall, you catch them, the score climbs: a complete game. Everything in Part 2 is an addition . 💾 Save your project before you stop Type Star Catcher in the title box above the stage. Signed in? Choose File → Save now ; it waits in My Stuff . Not signed in? Choose File → Save to your computer and note where the .sb3 file lands. Part 2 opens exactly this project.

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix The bowl won't move The stage lacks keyboard focus, or the ifs sit outside the forever Click the stage once; put both ifs inside the forever A star sits frozen at the top, or none appear The original is visible, or the clone script lacks show Original: hide first. Clone script: include show Stars pile up at the bottom Nothing removes missed stars yet Expected today; Part 2 fixes it Catch sound is cut off or silent The clone is deleted while its sound is still playing Use hide → play sound … until done → delete this clone Score doesn't reset on replay reset game isn't called, or it's inside the forever Put reset game right under the Bowl's green flag, before the forever Test after every step. If it worked a minute ago and doesn't now, the bug is almost certainly in the last thing you added.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Build it as a team
sections.text: The child directs; the parent types when needed Your child can own the decisions before they can do every drag. They're the director : they decide what the game is, how it looks, and whether a change is "right." You're the typist , taking the mouse only for fiddly bits and only when asked: "You're the boss of this game. I'm your helper. Tell me what you want, and if you want me to do a tricky part, just say 'your turn.'" When you do take the mouse, narrate and hand it straight back: "Okay, I'm finding 'change x by'... it's in blue Motion... snapping it inside the if. Your turn — press the flag and see if it worked!" Planning out loud Treat the design card as a conversation, not a form, and write their answers in their words: "If you explained this game to your friend, what would you say? How do you win? How do you lose? What's the one thing the player does most?" When a big idea arrives mid-build, park it kindly: "Ooh, rocks too? Someday list! We'll add it once the stars work." Play for a minute after every working step. "You do it" usually means it's time to save and stop. 👧 Ages 5–7 They draw the design card, choose sprites and sound, and press every green flag. You drag while they direct. Catching stars with a score is a complete game at this age. 🧒 Ages 8–11 They fill in the card and do most of the building. You read each step aloud and help nest blocks inside ifs and loops. 🧑 Ages 12+ Give them the card and checklist, not the steps. Let them work out the scripts, then explain the "star factory" back to you. 🌟 End on a high Finish with a high-score round: each of you plays once and your child writes the scores on the design card. A number to beat makes Part 2 something to look forward to.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: Your child has a huge game idea with dragons, shops, and ten levels. What's the best first move? Question 2: In Star Catcher, why does the original Star sprite hide and only make clones? Question 3: When a star is caught, why does the clone hide and play sound Pop until done before delete this clone ?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down Tape your design card in next to today's entry. Key concepts: What is the "smallest playable version," and why build it first? What clicked: Which piece fit better than expected: the star factory, reset game , or the catch check? Questions & confusion: Which of today's steps could you not yet rebuild from memory? Ideas to try: Which someday-list item do you want to add first in Part 2? Progress & feelings: How did director/typist feel? When was it hard not to grab the mouse? 💡 Teach It tip: Have your child glue the design card into their coder's notebook with today's best score beside it.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways Plan before you code: brainstorm, pick one small idea, sketch it, and list the pieces as a checklist. A design card turns an idea into a to-do list; a someday list keeps big ideas parked. Build the smallest playable version first, then add and test one feature at a time. A hidden original acts as a clone factory ; each clone falls, checks for a catch, and deletes itself. Your child directs; you type only when needed. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Planned a game on paper with a design card and checklist Built a playable Star Catcher with movement, clones, and score Used your own reset game My Block in a real project 📋 Before the Next Lesson Save the project as Star Catcher and check you can find it again Play a few rounds and write down the best score Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage We only got as far as the moving bowl. Are we behind? Not at all. Planning plus a working bowl is a solid sitting. Save it and start at step 5 next time. My child wants to make a totally different game instead. Is that okay? Yes, and it's a great sign. Use the same routine. Dodging, catching, and collecting games all use this clone-and-touching pattern, so the steps still apply. The stars piling up at the bottom bothers my child. Can we fix it now? If they're eager, peek at step 8 in the next lesson. Otherwise, call it a cliffhanger: "Next time, missed stars cost you!" 🔭 Looking Ahead In Lesson 4.4: Capstone Part 2 — Lives, Game Over & Launch Day , you'll open this saved project and finish it: missed stars cost lives, a game over broadcast stops everything, and a bonus comes off the someday list. Then comes launch day, when your child shows the game off. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You turned a paper plan into something your child can play. Going from nothing to something is the hardest half of any project, and you've done it. 🏠 Back to Course Home

label: Lesson 4.4
title: Capstone Part 2 — Lives, Game Over & Launch Day

sections.heading: 🎬 Where we left off
sections.text: First, open your saved project . If you saved online, click My Stuff (the folder icon at the top of scratch.mit.edu) and choose Star Catcher . If you saved a file, open the editor and choose File → Load from your computer , then pick the .sb3 file. Play one round together before touching any code. In Part 1 you built: Bowl: calls reset game , then slides with the arrow keys. Star (original): hides and keeps making clones. Star (each clone): falls, and if it touches the Bowl, scores and pops: when I start as a clone go to x: pick random -220 to 220 y: 170 show forever change y by -5 if touching Bowl? then change score by 1 hide play sound Pop until done delete this clone What's missing? Missed stars pile up, lives never changes, and the game never ends. Those are today's jobs.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Lives, Game Over & polish
sections.text: The numbering continues from Part 1, so today is steps 8–10 . Test after each one; with a child driving, expect about double the times shown. Missing a star costs a life (about 5 min) On the Star, add a second if inside the clone's forever loop, under the catching if . A clone that falls past the bowl takes a life and deletes itself; if that was the last life, it announces Game Over: when I start as a clone go to x: pick random -220 to 220 y: 170 show forever change y by -5 if touching Bowl? then change score by 1 hide play sound Pop until done delete this clone if y position < -170 then change lives by -1 if lives = 0 then broadcast game over delete this clone The green less than block is in Operators ; drop the blue y position reporter (bottom of Motion) into its left slot. For game over , open the broadcast dropdown and choose New message . Why check lives inside the star ? The star is the one that knows it was missed, so it's the natural place to notice the last life. delete this clone sits last in that if , so each miss costs exactly one life. Show GAME OVER (about 5 min) Click Paint (the brush under Choose a Sprite), write GAME OVER with the Text tool, and name the sprite Game Over . Give it two scripts: when ⚑ clicked hide when I receive game over go to front layer show stop all stop all freezes everything and removes every clone, but GAME OVER stays visible because it was shown first. The green flag hides it for the next game. Add music, then playtest and tune (about 7 min) Click the Stage (bottom right), open its Sounds tab, and choose a sound from the library's Loops category. Then give the Stage this script: when ⚑ clicked forever play sound your music loop until done Now play three games. Too hard? Change -5 to -3 , or lengthen the wait between stars. Too easy? Do the opposite. This is called tuning , and kids love it. ✅ Project Completion Tick these off together: ☐ The bowl moves left and right with the arrow keys ☐ The green flag resets score to 0 and lives to 3 (via reset game ) ☐ The original star stays hidden; clones fall from random spots ☐ Catching a star adds 1 to score and plays a sound ☐ A missed star removes 1 life and disappears ☐ At 0 lives, GAME OVER appears and everything stops ☐ Pressing the green flag again starts a fresh game ☐ The project is saved ( File → Save now , or Save to your computer )

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: Make it theirs
sections.text: Bring out the someday list. Your child picks one item, adds it, tests it, and only then picks another. 🌟 If you want to go further: stars speed up Make a speed variable; add set speed to 3 to reset game . Replace change y by -5 with change y by (0 − speed) , and add change speed by 0.2 next to change score by 1 . Every catch speeds things up. 🌟 If you want to go further: rocks to dodge Duplicate the Star and give it a rock costume. In its clone script, touching Bowl does change lives by -1 (plus the lives = 0 check) instead of scoring; a rock reaching the bottom just deletes itself. 🌟 If you want to go further: a high score Make a high score variable. In the Game Over sprite, before stop all , add if score > high score then set high score to score . Keep it out of reset game so it survives between games. 🌟 If you want to go further: levels Make a level variable, set to 1 in reset game . In the Bowl's forever loop, add if score = 10 and level = 1 then set level to 2, switch backdrop . Level 3 uses the same pattern with a bigger score.

sections.heading: 🚀 Launch Day
sections.text: When the checklist is complete, hold a launch. It takes five minutes, and it's what your child will remember: Pick a player. A sibling, grandparent, neighbor, or someone on a video call. The designer explains the rules first, just like on the design card: "Use the arrows. Catch stars. Don't miss three!" Hands off. Your child watches someone play their game; don't explain for them. Ask the player for one thing they liked and one idea. The idea goes on the someday list. Publishing to the Scratch website is a separate decision with its own safety choices. Lesson 5.2: Sharing Safely & the Scratch Community walks you through it; until then, show it off in person.

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix Stars still pile up at the bottom The y position < -170 check is outside the forever Put it inside the clone's forever loop, with delete this clone inside the if Lives drop by more than 1 per miss delete this clone isn't inside the lives if Make it the last block inside that if GAME OVER never shows Broadcast and receive messages don't match, or lives never reach exactly 0 Pick the same game over message in both; check reset game sets lives to 3 GAME OVER is showing when a new game starts The Game Over sprite has no green-flag hide Add when 🟩 clicked → hide to that sprite Music overlaps itself or stutters start sound used in the forever Use play sound … until done so each loop finishes first If it worked before step 8 and doesn't now, the bug is in step 8. That's the gift of building one piece at a time. 🌱 Growth mindset: finishing is its own skill The last stretch is often the hardest: the "wow" moments are behind you, and bugs feel personal because you're so close . That's normal. Name it out loud: "This is the finishing part. It's slower, and that's okay. One more fix." Kids who watch a grown-up push calmly through the last 10% learn that finishing is practiced, not inborn.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Finish strong
sections.text: The director/typist roles still apply. What's new is keeping energy up and handling frustration near the finish. Restart the momentum Don't open with "okay, step 8." Open by playing, which reminds your child they already made something that works: "Before we add anything — can you beat your high score from last time? Show me!" Stop on a win If energy fades, stop right after something works, never mid-bug. Step 8 working is a fine place to pause. When frustration hits near the end A broken game right before the finish can bring tears. Slow down and make the bug small: "It worked before we added this part, so the problem is only in this part. Let's read it together, one block at a time." If they're past the point of fun, it's fine to say "let's save it and fix it with fresh eyes tomorrow." That's a real programmer move. 👧 Ages 5–7 Lives are optional. If you add them, you build while they watch the number drop. They paint the GAME OVER sign and pick the music. Launch day is the star event. 🧒 Ages 8–11 They build steps 8–10 with you reading aloud. Let them do all the tuning, and let them choose one someday item on their own. 🧑 Ages 12+ Give them the checklist and let them finish solo. Then challenge them: plan a new game with a fresh design card, using the same routine. 🌟 End on a high Launch day is the high. Afterward, ask your child, "What was the hardest part, and how did you get past it?" Their answer is the real lesson of the capstone.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: Each missed star is taking away 2 or 3 lives instead of 1. What's the likely cause? Question 2: Why does the Game Over sprite show itself before running stop all ? Question 3: Right before the finish, the game breaks and your child is close to tears. Best move?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down This closes Module 4, so leave room for a look back at the whole project. Key concepts: In your own words, what does a broadcast do in Star Catcher, and why does the lives check live inside the star clone? What clicked: Which moment made it feel like a "real" game: the lives counting down, GAME OVER appearing, or the music? Questions & confusion: Which part could you not yet rebuild from memory? Ideas to try: What did your launch-day player suggest? What would your child's next game be? Progress & feelings: Looking back over all of Module 4 (clones, My Blocks, and a two-part game), what are you proudest of? How did your child's confidence change from Part 1 to launch day? 💡 Teach It tip: Have your child add a drawing or screenshot of the finished game, with their best score and their launch-day player's name, next to the design card. It's page one of their game design portfolio.

sections.heading: Summary & Module 4 Complete 🎉
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways A clone can check its own fate: missed stars subtract a life and delete themselves. A broadcast lets one sprite tell another "it's over"; show the sign, then stop all . Tuning numbers is how a working game becomes a fun one. Start second sittings by playing, stop on a win, and shrink bugs to the last change. Launch day turns "I made a game" into "people play my game." 🏆 You finished Module 4! Clones, custom blocks, and a complete game taken from a paper plan to launch day with your child. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Finished Star Catcher with score, lives, and Game Over Used a broadcast and stop all to end a game cleanly Held a launch day with a real player 📋 Before the Next Lesson Tick every box on the Project Completion checklist Add one someday item, or start a design card for your child's own game Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage I ended up doing most of the building. Is that a problem? It's common in a first capstone. What matters is who made the decisions : if your child chose the idea, sprites, sounds, and tuning, it's their game. Next time, hand over one more step; that's what the next lesson is about. Should we publish it on the Scratch website? Not yet. Sharing is a great goal, but read Lesson 5.2 first so you can make the choice together with the safety settings in mind. My child wants to keep adding features forever. Should I stop them? No, that's the best outcome! Keep the rhythm: one feature, test, save. If it gets tangled, call this version "done" and start Star Catcher 2. 🔭 Looking Ahead Next comes the other half of this course: Module 5: Teaching Scratch to Your Child . It opens with Lesson 5.1: The Art of Not Taking Over , on the hardest part of coaching: keeping your hands off the mouse. You'll learn what to say instead of fixing it yourself, so the win belongs to your child. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You started this course unsure what a sprite was. Now you've planned a game, built it over two sittings, and watched someone play it. That's what game designers do. Keep the design card somewhere you'll see it. 🏠 Back to Course Home

label: Lesson 5.1
title: The Art of Not Taking Over

sections.heading: Why "not taking over" matters
sections.text: When we grab the mouse and fix the bug, we get a working project — and rob our child of the exact moment learning happens. The struggle is the lesson. Your goal isn't a polished project; it's a child who believes "I can figure things out." Every time you solve it for them, you quietly teach: "this is too hard for you." Every time you help them solve it themselves, you teach: "you are a person who solves hard things."

sections.heading: 🎓 Scaffolding: help that fades
sections.text: Scaffolding means giving just enough support to keep your child moving, then removing it bit by bit as they gain confidence — like training wheels you gradually raise. Aim to give the least help that unblocks them. Too little help Just-right (scaffold) Too much help "Figure it out." (walks away) "Which category might have a 'move' block?" "Drag the blue move block here." (or does it) Child stalls, gives up Child stays in the driver's seat Child becomes a spectator

sections.heading: 🎓 Ask, don't tell
sections.text: Questions keep your child thinking; answers end the thinking. Build a small toolkit of go-to prompts: Your question toolkit "What do you want to happen?" "What happened instead ?" "Which block do you think is in charge of that?" "What could we try to test that idea?" "Where have we seen something like this before?" Notice none of these give the answer. They hand your child the next step of thinking — which is the real skill. ⚠️ The "helpful" reflex to resist You'll see the fix instantly and want to blurt it out. Pause. Count to five. Ask a question instead. That five-second gap is where your child's problem-solving muscle grows.

sections.heading: 🎓 Praise the process, not the talent
sections.text: Decades of research (Carol Dweck's work on "growth mindset") show what we praise shapes how kids handle challenge. Praise fixed traits ("you're so smart") and kids avoid risks that might prove otherwise. Praise effort and strategy and they lean into hard things. ✅ Say this "You kept trying different things until it worked." "That was clever how you tested one block at a time." "You didn't give up when it got tricky." "How did you figure that out?" ⚠️ Go easy on this "You're a genius!" "You're so naturally good at this." "See, that was easy!" (it wasn't, to them) Praising only the finished product 🌱 Growth mindset: teach your child the power of "yet" So far in this course, "yet" has been a word for you . Now hand it to your child. When they say "I can't make the stars fall," add one word: "You can't make them fall… yet ." That tiny word turns a verdict into a to-do list. Say it often enough and you'll hear them start saying it to themselves. Pair it with process praise. "You're so smart!" feels kind, but it quietly tells a child that success proves smartness — so the next bug feels like proof of the opposite. "You tested one block at a time until you found it" tells them what they did , which is something they can do again. Try explaining it to them plainly: "Your brain is like a muscle — it grows when things are tricky, not when they're easy. When coding feels hard, that's your brain getting stronger. You haven't figured it out yet ." And model it: let them hear you say, "I got stuck on clones at first too — I just kept trying things." Your honest struggle is the most convincing lesson in the room.

sections.heading: 🎓 Productive struggle (the good kind)
sections.text: There's a sweet spot between "so easy it's boring" and "so hard it's crushing." In that zone — sometimes called productive struggle or "flow" — kids are challenged but capable. Your job is to keep them in it. Bored? Raise the bar: "What if it kept score?" "Can you add a second level?" Frustrated? Shrink the step: "Let's just get it to move first. One thing at a time." Boiling over? Take a break — a real, respected debugging strategy, not a failure.

sections.heading: 🎓 Keeping the spark alive
sections.text: Follow their interests. A kid who loves cats will out-code any assignment about spreadsheets. Let the projects be theirs . Keep sessions short and positive. End on a win, not on a bug. 20–30 focused minutes beats a grinding hour. Make it social. Have them demo to a grandparent or friend. An audience is rocket fuel. Let it be silly. Fart sounds and exploding cats are perfectly valid computer science. Joy is the goal. Model your own learning. "I don't know either — let's find out together" is one of the most powerful things you can say. 💡 You don't have to know the answer Being a great coding parent isn't about expertise — it's about curiosity and encouragement. "Let's figure it out together" models exactly the mindset you're trying to grow.

sections.heading: 🎯 Quick Check
sections.text: Question 1: What is "scaffolding" in teaching? Question 2: Which praise best builds resilience? Question 3: Your child is bored because the task is too easy. Best response?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down This lesson has no code, so your journal is where the practice happens. Be honest — nobody is grading your parenting. Key concepts: In your own words, what is scaffolding ? What's the difference between praising the process and praising the person ? What clicked: Think back to building Star Catcher or an earlier project together. Was there a moment you grabbed the mouse? What might a guiding question have sounded like instead? Questions & confusion: Where is the line between "productive struggle" and "too frustrated" for your child? What signs tell you they've crossed it? Ideas to try: Pick two questions from the toolkit and one "yet" sentence you'll use in your next session. Write them on a sticky note for the computer. Progress & feelings: Which is harder for you — staying quiet when you see the fix, or watching your child struggle? Why do you think that is? 💡 Teach It tip: Invite your child to add a "Yet List" page to their coder's notebook: things they can't do in Scratch yet . Revisit it every few weeks and let them cross items off — nothing makes growth more visible.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways The struggle is the lesson — resist fixing it for them. Scaffold : give the least help that unblocks, then fade it. Ask guiding questions; praise effort and strategy, not talent. Keep them in "productive struggle," follow their interests, and end on a win. Teach the word "yet" — and model it with your own mistakes. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Learned the scaffolding ladder: I lead → they lead → they teach Built a question toolkit to replace ready-made answers Swapped talent praise for process praise and "yet" Learned to spot boredom vs. frustration and adjust the challenge 📋 Before the Next Lesson Run one Scratch session where you keep your hands off the mouse the whole time Use at least one "yet" and one process-praise sentence out loud Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage My child just wants me to do it for them. What do I do? That's very common, especially after a frustrating stretch. Offer to be their "hands" while they're the "boss": you drag only the blocks they name and point to. They still do all the thinking, and within a session or two most kids want the mouse back. Isn't it unkind to watch them struggle when I know the answer? Watching them struggle alone would be. Staying next to them, asking questions, and shrinking the step when needed is the opposite — it's support that trusts them. If tears start, take a break; that's a respected strategy, not a failure. I've said "you're so smart" a thousand times. Have I done damage? Not at all — kids are resilient, and warmth matters more than perfect wording. Simply start adding process praise alongside it ("…and I love how you kept testing"). The shift happens over months, not in a single sentence. 🔭 Looking Ahead As your child grows more confident, they'll want to share their creations with the world. In Lesson 5.2: Sharing Safely & the Scratch Community , we set that up safely — accounts, privacy, the moderated community, comments, and healthy habits. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey Sitting on your hands is genuinely hard — you'll slip, and that's fine. Every time you catch yourself and ask a question instead, you're giving your child something more lasting than a working project: the belief that they can figure things out.

sections.heading: 🎓 Accounts & privacy
sections.text: Scratch is run by a non-profit and takes children's privacy seriously (it complies with children's privacy laws like COPPA in the US). When your child signs up, Scratch asks for a parent/guardian email and collects minimal information. Figure 1: The official Scratch for Parents page — your best reference for privacy and safety specifics, straight from the source. ✅ Set up the account the safe way Use a username that hides real identity (no full name, school, or birth year). Enter your email as the parent contact — you'll get account notices. Choose a password together and keep it somewhere you both can find it. Remind them: never share real name, address, school, phone, or photos in projects or comments.

sections.heading: 🎓 Private by default
sections.text: A crucial reassurance: projects are NOT public until your child explicitly clicks “Share.” Everything they build stays private to their account until then. Nothing is broadcast to the world by accident. 💡 You can code without ever sharing If you'd rather keep everything private for now, that's completely fine — your child can create, save, and enjoy Scratch indefinitely without sharing a single project. Sharing is a choice, not a requirement.

sections.heading: 🎓 The moderated community
sections.text: When a project is shared, others can view it, "love" it, favorite it, remix it, and comment. Scratch works hard to keep this space kind: there's active moderation, community guidelines, and easy reporting. Figure 2: The Community Guidelines — short, kid-readable, and worth reading together. The guidelines boil down to a few kind, sensible rules: Be respectful — treat others how you'd want to be treated. Be constructive — give helpful feedback, not put-downs. Keep personal info private — yours and everyone else's. Be honest — credit others' work when you remix. Help keep the site friendly — report anything that isn't.

sections.heading: 🎓 Comments & controls
sections.text: Comments are the main way kids interact. A few things that make this safer than typical social media: Control What it does Report button Flags any comment or project for the moderation team. Turn comments off Your child can disable comments on their own projects entirely. Delete comments They control comments on their projects and profile. Block/ignore Unwanted interactions can be reported and users blocked. No private messaging There are no hidden DMs — interactions are public and visible to you. ⚠️ It's still the internet Moderation is strong but not perfect, and any social space can bring criticism or the occasional unkind comment. Keep the account on a shared device or in a common room, check in regularly, and make it normal to show you a mean comment so you can report it together.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Digital citizenship
sections.text: Scratch is many kids' first online community — a wonderful, low-stakes place to practice being a good digital citizen, with you alongside. The conversation to have before sharing "When we share your project, other kids around the world can see it and leave comments. Most are super nice! But our family rules are: we never share private stuff — our real name, where we live, our school — and if anyone's ever unkind, you show me and we handle it together. Deal?" Model kind commenting Write a comment together on a project you both like. Praise something specific: "I love how the dragon breathes fire — how did you do that?" Kind, curious, specific — the gold standard. Handle criticism gracefully Someone will eventually leave a "meh" comment. Frame it early: "Not everyone will love everything we make, and that's okay. We can learn from helpful notes and ignore unkind ones." 👧 Ages 5–7 Keep it private, or share only with family. They don't need the public community yet — focus on making. 🧒 Ages 8–11 Good age to start sharing with your supervision . Read comments together at first. Practice writing kind ones. 🧑 Ages 12+ More independence, with clear expectations. Talk about online reputation, crediting remixes, and not oversharing. 🌱 Growth mindset: feedback is information, not a verdict Sharing is the first time your child's work meets strangers' opinions — and the first time many of us parents feel that sting on their behalf. Help them sort comments into two piles: helpful ("the jump is hard to time") is information they can use to make version 2 better; unkind says more about the commenter than the project. Neither one decides whether they're "good at coding." Model it with your own work: share a small project of yours , read the comments together, and think out loud — "Hmm, that's a fair point. I haven't figured out how to fix that yet." Every real Scratcher's best project started as a version 1 someone had ideas about.

sections.heading: 🎓 Healthy habits
sections.text: Balance making vs. browsing. Creating is the goal; endless scrolling through others' games less so. Nudge toward "let's make" over "let's watch." Time boundaries. Agree on session lengths up front, just like any screen time. Shared space. Keep Scratch on a family device or in a common area, especially early on. Regular check-ins. "Show me what you made!" doubles as fun bonding and light supervision. Know the off switch. You can review your child's account via the parent email and Scratch's account tools whenever you like.
