sections.text: Question 1: When is a child's Scratch project visible to the public? Question 2: Which is TRUE about the Scratch community? Question 3: Best safety habit for a young sharer?

sections.heading: 📓 Learning Journal
sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down This one is part journal, part family plan. What you write here can become your household's sharing rules. Key concepts: In your own words, what does "private until shared" mean? What protections does the Scratch community have that typical social media doesn't? What clicked: Which fact most eased (or sharpened) a worry you had about kids online — no private messaging, turning comments off, the report button? Questions & confusion: What would you still like to check on the official Scratch for Parents page before your child shares? Ideas to try: Draft your three or four family sharing rules (what never gets shared, where Scratch is used, what to do with a mean comment). Which project would be a good first one to share together? Progress & feelings: How do you feel about your child being part of an online community — excited, nervous, both? How did they react to the "before sharing" conversation? 💡 Teach It tip: Write the family sharing rules together on one page of your child's coder's notebook and have them sign it. Kids keep rules they helped write far better than rules handed to them.

sections.heading: Summary & What's Next
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways Scratch minimizes data, uses a parent email, and is built for kids' privacy. Projects are private until shared — sharing is always a choice. The community is moderated, guideline-based, and has no private messaging. Set a non-identifying username, keep it a shared space, and talk about kind, safe behavior. For the definitive, up-to-date details, always check the official Scratch for Parents and Privacy Policy pages. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Learned how Scratch accounts, privacy, and the parent email work Confirmed that nothing goes public until your child clicks Share Know the community guidelines and every comment control Have a script for the "before sharing" family conversation 📋 Before the Next Lesson Set up (or review) your child's account with a non-identifying username and your email Read the Community Guidelines together Write your family sharing rules and your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage Does my child need an account at all? No. Anyone can open the editor and create without signing in, then use File → Save to your computer . An account adds saving online, sharing, and the community — worth it when you're ready, but never required. Should my child share Star Catcher, since it started from the course? Absolutely — it's their game, built with their choices. If it began as a remix of someone else's project, Scratch shows the credit automatically; it's still good manners to add a thank-you in the Notes and Credits box. Crediting others is part of good digital citizenship. What if my child gets an unkind comment? Stay calm and treat it as a team job: read it together, report it with the Report button, delete it from their project, and talk about how it made them feel. Remind them the comment doesn't measure their work — and consider turning comments off on that project for a while. 🔭 Looking Ahead Your child is coding, creating, and sharing safely. But what about a younger sibling who can't read the blocks yet? In Lesson 5.3: ScratchJr — Coding for Ages 5–7 , you'll learn the free picture-block app built for little ones, and how to coach a pre-reader through their first program. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey Worrying about your child online means you're paying attention — that's exactly the job. You now know more about how Scratch keeps kids safe than most parents ever look up. Trust the plan you've made, keep checking in, and let them enjoy the audience they've earned.

sections.heading: 🎬 Meet ScratchJr
sections.text: ScratchJr is a free app for children about 5 to 7, on iPads, Android tablets, and Chromebooks. Kids snap blocks together just like in Scratch, but every block is a picture , so a child who can't read yet can still code. Figure 1: The ScratchJr website, with download links and guides for parents and teachers. By the end of this lesson you'll have built this: tap the pet, and it hops, grows, and says hello in your child's own recorded voice . 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 🎙️ My Sound 🔽 Shrink 2 ⏹️ End 💡 Before you start Install ScratchJr from your tablet's app store (free, no ads or in-app purchases). Open it, tap the house icon, then the big + to start a new project.

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: How ScratchJr differs from Scratch
sections.text: The big ideas carry over: events start scripts, blocks run in order, loops repeat. What changes is everything that would trip up a small child. Scratch ScratchJr Block direction Stack top to bottom Snap side by side, read left to right like a sentence Reading Every block has words Blocks show pictures ; only a few, like “Say,” take typed words Device Computer browser Made for tablets : tap and drag with a finger Numbers “Steps” (tiny units) Grid squares a child can count Sharing Online community Projects stay on the device , with no public community That last row is a quiet gift for parents: no comments, followers, or strangers. (The community safety habits from Lesson 5.2 can wait until your child moves up to Scratch.)

sections.heading: 🎓 Learn It: Six colors of picture blocks
sections.text: Tap a colored button on the left of the block area and that category's blocks slide into view. Color tells you what a block does: 🟡 Triggering 🔵 Motion 🟣 Looks 🟢 Sound 🟠 Control 🔴 End Color What it does Blocks you'll use most 🟡 Triggering Starts a script Start on Green Flag, Start on Tap, Start on Bump (touching another character) 🔵 Motion Moves the character Move right/left/up/down, Turn, Hop, Go Home 🟣 Looks Changes how it looks Say, Grow, Shrink, Reset Size, Hide, Show 🟢 Sound Makes noise Pop, plus sounds you record 🟠 Control Timing and repetition Wait, Set Speed, Repeat 🔴 End Caps the script End, Repeat Forever, Go to Page The small number under a Motion block counts grid squares . Tap the grid button above the stage, and “Move right 3” becomes something a child can count with a finger. 🎨 Watch out: the colors don't match Scratch In Scratch, green is Operators and sound is pink. In ScratchJr, green is Sound and yellow starts things. Kids won't care, but it can confuse you when switching apps. Trust the pictures.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: “My Pet Says Hi”
sections.text: Build this yourself first (about ten minutes) so you know where everything is before you sit down with your child. Pick or make a pet Tap the + beside the character list and choose an animal, or tap the paintbrush to draw one. The paint editor's camera tool fills a shape with a photo. Kids love putting their own face on a character. Start on tap Tap the yellow button and drag Start on Tap (a finger touching a character) into the script area. The script now runs whenever someone taps the pet. Hop and grow From blue , drag Hop so it snaps onto the right side of the trigger. From purple , snap Grow on after it. Tap the pet to test. 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 Record a sound Tap green , then the microphone block. Press record, say “Hi! I'm your pet!” (or bark, or giggle), stop, and accept it. Snap the new sound block on after Grow. Shrink back and end Add a purple Shrink so the pet returns to normal size (otherwise it grows with every tap), then cap the row with the red End block. 👆 Start on Tap ⤴️ Hop 2 🔼 Grow 2 🎙️ My Sound 🔽 Shrink 2 ⏹️ End ✅ Tap the pet! It hops, puffs up, says hi in a real voice, and settles back down: an event, a sequence, and a sound, the same thinking as your first Scratch cat laid out sideways.

sections.heading: 🛠️ Try It: A two-page story
sections.text: A ScratchJr project can have up to four pages , like a picture book, each with its own background and characters. Add page 2 Tap the + in the page strip on the right. Pick a background for the new page and add a character. On page 1, turn the page Back on page 1, give the pet a green-flag script that ends with Go to Page , which appears in the red End category once a second page exists. 🏁 Start on Green Flag 💬 Say Come to my house! ⏱️ Wait 10 📄 Go to Page 2 On page 2, say hello Give page 2's character a green-flag script too. When the story turns to a page, that page's green-flag scripts start. 🏁 Start on Green Flag ➡️ Move Right 3 💬 Say Welcome home! ⏹️ End Press the green flag and watch the story play across two pages.

sections.heading: 🐛 Common problems & fixes
sections.text: What you see Likely cause Fix Tapping the pet does nothing Script starts with Green Flag, or a block isn't snapped on Use Start on Tap ; drag blocks until they click into one row The pet keeps getting bigger Grow with no Shrink Add Shrink (same number) or Reset Size at the end The pet walks off the stage Moves add up each run Start the row with the blue Go Home block Recording is silent No microphone permission Allow the microphone for ScratchJr in the tablet's settings A block “vanished” It was dragged back onto the palette, which deletes it Drag a fresh one out; no harm done 🌱 Growth mindset: wobbly is what learning looks like Your five-year-old will drop blocks in the wrong spot, and you may find sideways rows odd after weeks of Scratch. That's experimenting, not failing. When a script flops, laugh: “Whoa, that's not what we planned! What should we try?” A child who hears that at five learns that surprises are interesting, not scary.

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Coding with a very young child
sections.text: Five-year-olds have short attention, fingers still learning to drag, and huge imaginations. Plan around all three. Keep sessions short: 10–15 minutes Stop while it's still fun, ideally after a big laugh, and they'll ask to do it again tomorrow. Tell the story first, then code it Before touching the tablet, ask for a tiny story out loud: who is in it and what happens . Then turn each event into a block. “So the puppy jumps, gets really big, and barks. Which picture looks like jumping? …Yes, the hop! What comes next?” You read, they tap You read anything with words aloud. They tap, drag, and press the green flag. Keep your hands in your lap; if a drag keeps missing, steady the tablet rather than doing it for them. Let them record silly sounds The microphone is the most motivating feature in the app. Burps, animal noises, “I'm a dinosaur!”: hearing their own voice come out of a character they coded is pure magic. “You made the puppy do that! You told it what to do, and it listened. That's what coders do.” 👶 Ages 4–5 Sit them on your lap like a shared picture book. You set up the character; they pick from two or three blocks you point to and do all the tapping. One trigger plus two blocks is plenty. 👧 Ages 5–6 They drag and snap while you sit beside them. Build “My Pet Says Hi” together, then ask, “What else could it do when you tap it?” Count grid squares together for Move blocks. 🧒 Ages 6–7 Give a goal, not steps: “Make a story with two pages.” Let them draw characters and try Repeat or Start on Bump, then read their row back to you, left to right. 🌟 End with a show Use full-screen mode and have them “perform” their story for the family, tapping the pet on cue. Applause and an encore beat any sticker chart. 🚀 When to move up to Scratch Readiness matters more than age, though most kids are ready around 7 or 8 . Look for comfortable reading of short labels, a mouse or trackpad they can handle, and requests ScratchJr can't meet (like keeping score). When you switch, bridge it: “Remember the yellow start blocks? In Scratch they're Events, and the blocks stack like a tower.” Then start with Lesson 1.3 's moving, talking cat.

sections.text: Take five minutes to write it down A notebook or a sticky note on the fridge works. Your notes will help you plan the next session. Key concepts: How is a ScratchJr row like a Scratch stack, and how is it different? What clicked: Did counting grid squares or hearing a recorded voice make a coding idea feel simpler? Questions & confusion: What tripped you up (the mismatched colors, pages, the microphone)? Check it before your child sits down. Ideas to try: Jot down one tiny story your child could turn into a two-page project. Progress & feelings: How did it feel to keep your hands in your lap, and what made your child laugh? 💡 Teach It tip: Young kids can journal too. Have them draw their pet and what it did, and write their words underneath. Months later, those drawings show how they grew.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways ScratchJr is a free tablet app for ages 5–7 with picture blocks, so no reading is needed. Blocks snap into a horizontal row read left to right, in six colors: yellow Triggering, blue Motion, purple Looks, green Sound, orange Control, red End. Projects have up to four pages , turned with Go to Page , and stay on the device. Coach in 10–15-minute sessions: story first, you read, they tap, lots of silly sounds. Move up to Scratch around 7–8 , when reading is comfortable and they want more. 🏅 What You've Accomplished Built a tap-to-talk pet with a recorded sound Made a two-page story with Go to Page Planned a coaching style for a very young child 📋 Before the Next Lesson Install ScratchJr on a tablet your child can use Do one 10-minute “My Pet Says Hi” session together Write your journal entry ❓ Common Questions at This Stage My child is 4. Is that too young for ScratchJr? Not if you're sitting together. Keep it very short and focus on tapping and recording sounds. If it isn't fun yet, try again in a few months. We don't have a tablet. Can we use ScratchJr on a laptop? ScratchJr is built for tablets and Chromebooks. On a regular computer, use full Scratch and follow the Ages 5–7 tips in each lesson: you read, they choose and press the green flag. My 6-year-old wants to use Scratch like an older sibling. Should I say no? No need. Let them try; if it frustrates them, offer ScratchJr as “your own coding app.” The concepts are the same, so time in either counts. 🔭 Looking Ahead In the course finale, Lesson 5.4: What Comes After Scratch , you'll map the road ahead: going deeper in Scratch, coding real-world gadgets, and the bridge from blocks to typed languages like Python. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You learned to make coding fit a child who can't even read yet. That flexibility is the heart of great teaching, and your little one is lucky to have you as their first coding buddy. 🏠 Back to Course Home

sections.heading: 🗺️ The coding road map
sections.text: There's no single "correct" path — it depends on your child's age and interests. Here's the lay of the land: The key idea: the concepts transfer . Sequences, loops, conditionals, variables, and events exist in every language. Your child already knows them — later tools just change the syntax.

sections.heading: 🎓 For younger kids: ScratchJr recap
sections.text: You covered this in depth in Lesson 5.3: ScratchJr — Coding for Ages 5–7 . The one-line version: ScratchJr is the free tablet app where blocks are pictures instead of words, so a 5–7-year-old (or any child who finds reading in Scratch tough) can code without reading. It's the start of the road map above — and a natural stepping stone up to full Scratch when they're ready. If you have a younger sibling in the house, revisit Lesson 5.3 for the coaching tips; they're a great chance for your older child to play teacher.

sections.heading: 🎓 Going deeper in Scratch
sections.text: Your child may spend years in Scratch alone — it has surprising depth. You've already climbed two of the big steps together; here's what you've got and what's still ahead. ✅ Already in your toolkit 🧬 Clones You met these in Lesson 4.1 and used them for Star Catcher's falling stars. Next step: make a variable "for this sprite only" so each clone keeps its own speed or health. 🧩 My Blocks You built your own blocks in Lesson 4.2 — like Star Catcher's reset game . Next step: go back through an old project and replace every repeated chunk of blocks with a well-named custom block that takes inputs — the same clean-up professional programmers call refactoring . 🔭 Still ahead 📋 Lists Store many values (high scores, inventory, quiz questions) — variables' bigger sibling. Find them under Variables → Make a List . 🧰 Extensions Click the Add Extension button (bottom-left of the editor) for new block categories: Pen (draw on the stage), Music (instruments and drums), Text to Speech , Video Sensing , and micro:bit . 🎨 Costumes & the paint editor Draw original characters and multi-frame animations from scratch. 🎮 Bigger games Levels, boss fights, menus — the same clones, My Blocks, variables, and broadcasts from Star Catcher, just more of them. The official Scratch Ideas page has step-by-step tutorials for all of these.

sections.heading: 🎓 Beyond the screen: physical computing
sections.text: Coding gets extra magical when it moves real things. These pair beautifully with Scratch: Tool What it does Great for Makey Makey Turns bananas, foil, playdough into keyboard keys Playful invention, ages 7+ micro:bit A tiny programmable board with lights & sensors; works with Scratch through the micro:bit extension Hands-on projects, ages 9+ LEGO robotics Motors & sensors you program to move Builders, ages 8+ Suddenly code controls the physical world — a huge motivator for kids who love building.

sections.heading: 🎓 The bridge to text code
sections.text: Eventually many kids grow curious about "real" typed code. The transition is smoother than you'd think, because they already own the concepts. Scratch (blocks) repeat 3 say Hi! Python (text) for i in range(3): print("Hi!") Same loop, same idea — just typed. Good first text languages: Python (friendly and popular), or JavaScript (makes web pages interactive). Gentle bridges: tools that show blocks and the equivalent text side-by-side help a lot. No rush. Many kids happily stay in Scratch through their early teens. Follow their curiosity, not a timetable. 🌱 Growth mindset: every new tool starts at "beginner" again The first week in Python — or with a micro:bit, or even the Pen extension — will feel clumsy, just like your first hour of dragging blocks did in Module 1. That dip isn't going backward; it's what learning something new always feels like. Remind your child (and yourself): "We couldn't make the cat move at first either. We can't do this yet ." You now have proof that it works. Seventeen lessons ago, clones and custom blocks were a mystery. The same patience that got you here will carry you through whatever comes next.

sections.heading: 🔗 Trusted next resources
sections.text: Scratch Ideas & Tutorials — official, step-by-step, free. Scratch offline app — code without internet (Windows, Mac, ChromeOS, Android). ScratchJr — for ages 5–7 (see Lesson 5.3 ). micro:bit — physical computing that works with Scratch. Code.org — free courses across ages, including block-based and beyond. Your local library or school often runs free coding clubs — ask around!

sections.heading: 💬 Teach It: Keep the momentum
sections.text: The best "next step" is almost always one more project your child is excited about. Depth of interest beats rushing to the next tool. Follow the fire. Loves animation? Do more animation. Loves games? Build the next game. Interest sustains itself. Set gentle challenges. "Could you add a second level?" keeps growth happening without pressure. Find a community. A coding club, a cousin who codes, or Scratch's own community gives them peers and an audience. Celebrate the journey. Look back at their first three-block cat versus what they build now. Growth is a powerful motivator to see. "Look how far you've come — remember when we made the cat just say hello? Now look what you can build. What do you want to make next?" 💡 And keep being the buddy Even as they surpass you (they will!), your encouragement, your curiosity, and your "show me what you made" stay just as valuable. You don't need to keep up with the code to keep cheering the coder.

sections.text: Your final entry: look back, then look ahead Before you write anything, flip back to your very first entry — the "why" page from Lesson 1.1 . Read it slowly. Then answer these. Whole-course reflection Your why: What did you hope to create with your child back then? Did you make it — or something even better? Your worry: Reread the worry you wrote down. How big does it feel now? Cross it off if you've earned it. Your number: In Lesson 1.1 you rated your confidence from 1–10. What's your number today? What moved it most? What clicked: Looking back over all seventeen lessons, which moment made you feel like a real coder — the first moving cat, the first working loop, the first falling clone, the finished game? Questions & confusion: What do you still want to learn? Lists? Extensions? Text code? Write it down — that's your next course. Ideas to try: Name the next project your child is excited about, and which path on the road map it leads toward. Ask them to pick their favorite page and tell you the story of that project — then start a fresh page titled "What I'll make next."

sections.heading: Course Complete 🎓🏆 You did it — Module 5 and the whole course!
sections.text: 🎓 Key Takeaways ScratchJr serves younger kids; the free offline app serves no-internet situations. You already have clones and My Blocks; lists and extensions (Pen, Music, micro:bit) are the next layers, and Scratch extends to hardware . The concepts transfer to text languages like Python — the jump is mostly syntax. Momentum comes from interest: one more exciting project beats rushing ahead. Seventeen lessons, five modules. You went from never having coded to learning Scratch, building a real game with clones and custom blocks, teaching your child, and guiding them safely into a whole community of young creators. That's an extraordinary gift to give a kid — and yourself. Now go make something wonderful together. 🐱💛 🏅 What You've Accomplished Module 1: met Scratch, toured the editor, and wrote your first program Module 2: mastered sequences, loops, and conditionals Module 3: built an animated story and a scoring game, then debugged and remixed Module 4: learned clones and My Blocks, and built Star Catcher together Module 5: became a coach, set up safe sharing, met ScratchJr, and mapped the road ahead 📋 Before Your Next Project Write your final journal entry and reread your first one Download the offline app if you'll code without internet Let your child choose the next project and one new thing to try (a list or an extension) ❓ Common Questions at This Stage My child is already better at Scratch than I am. Is my job done? Your job changes, it doesn't end. You don't have to keep up with the code to keep asking "show me what you made," "how did you do that?", and "what's next?" Being their audience and their question-asker stays valuable for years. When should we switch to Python? When your child is curious about it — not on a schedule. Typing fluency and reading comfort help, so many kids start around 10–13, but plenty stay happily in Scratch longer. Nothing they learn in Scratch is wasted; it all carries over. We took a long break and forgot things. Should we start the course over? No need. Skim the Key Takeaways of the lessons you want to refresh and rebuild one small project, like the Lesson 1.3 cat. It comes back much faster the second time — that's how learning works. 🔭 Looking Ahead This is the last lesson, but not the last project. The road ahead is yours to choose: one more Scratch game with a high-score list , a drawing toy with the Pen extension, a banana piano with a Makey Makey, or a first Python loop. Pick the one your child's eyes light up for, and start there. 💛 Encouragement for the Journey You started this course unsure whether you were "techy enough." You finished it having written programs, fixed bugs, built a game, and — most importantly — shown your child that grown-ups learn hard things too. That lesson will outlast every block you dragged.
